extracted.intended_audience: mathematics department faculty, chairs, and administrators responsible for undergraduate curriculum reform and assessment
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, implementing, and assessing department-level undergraduate mathematics curriculum reforms and programs (including cohort comparisons, advising/support interventions, and assessment instruments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcript analysis criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcript analyses gathered information on three criteria: fulfillment of university general education requirements; fulfillment of upper-division major requirements; fulfillment of mathematics requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to identify deficits that delay graduation (e.g., seniors lacking calculus). Can be applied across campuses to quantify 'bulge' effects; useful as an objective baseline metric for timeliness-to-degree analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student interview issues affecting progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Student responses centered on the following issues: course availability; course repeating; inaccurate or unhelpful advising; problems associated with isolation; financial and personal issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews help explain quantitative transcript findings. Transfer students reported the non-financial issues (first four) far more often than non-transfer students, indicating intervention targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch transfer students early
rubrics_metrics.description: “Catch” transfer students early. Academic departments identifying, contacting, and meeting with transfer students early in their university career may eliminate some of the problems later as seniors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: transfers often arrive with hidden deficits and feel isolated. Early contact can ensure correct course placement, build connections, and reduce later bottlenecks (quote: 'Care for your own wounded').

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accurate academic advising within the department
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide accurate academic advising within the department. Having the academic department individually advise students throughout their enrollment at the university may be extremely helpful in streamlining their paths to graduation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advising should cover specific requirements, prerequisites, scheduling, and referrals to support programs; reduces misadvising that leads to unnecessary courses or missing needed courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide effective academic support for key courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide effective academic support for key courses, such as Treisman workshop-style groups, together with scheduling key classes to accommodate student needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support may be required participation; workshop-style peer/cooperative learning has shown higher on-time completion and graduation rates. Scheduling should accommodate 'off-semester' transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department as the key element for student success
rubrics_metrics.description: The academic department is the key element in facilitating changes that will make a real difference for students, especially in providing advising and creative scheduling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departments should lead interventions, pair SEM faculty with student-support staff, and customize campus plans; evidence from multiple studies supports departmental-led programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-perspective evaluation framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate curriculum change from three perspectives: (1) reform (how the change fits national recommendations), (2) implementation process, and (3) comparison of student cohorts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framework structures data collection and analysis; use literature review and interviews for context, and cohort data (tests, grades, questionnaires) for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Fullan model (initiation, implementation, continuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Fullan's model: educational change has three phases—initiation, implementation, and continuation—all leading to outcomes; analyze factors for each phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both 'what to change' (alignment with reform goals) and 'how to change' (leadership, consensus-building, sustaining practices). Use Fullan factors to diagnose and support change processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary outcomes: student achievement and attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcomes for evaluation were student achievement and attitudes toward mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are necessary to judge reform, but attitude measurement requires careful, standardized instruments; lack of comparable attitude data can make cohort comparisons infeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design assessment instruments to mirror program goals
rubrics_metrics.description: All assessment instruments are designed to address course and program objectives and thereby measure student growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize program goals into measurable objectives (threads/content) so assessments directly map to desired growth; aligns instrument design, course objectives, and rubric interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori experimental design for cohort comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental design is needed before-the-fact for instruments to be compared; post-hoc comparisons are like comparing apples and oranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If comparisons across cohorts are intended, standardize instruments, quizzes, and questionnaires in advance; otherwise, data may be informative only within one cohort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grades in follow-on standardized courses as evaluation metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of grades in follow-on courses (e.g., physics and engineering science) can show meaningful downstream effects of curriculum change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardized, stable follow-on courses provide compelling evidence (statistical tests reported: chi-square, t-tests). Use courses with consistent content/standards year-to-year for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use portfolios to measure conceptual growth over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolios used since 1993 mostly as self-evaluation instruments; include common questions each semester and prior responses to show individual growth across courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require brief reflective responses (paragraphs) tied to program threads; maintaining prior responses in subsequent portfolios provides snapshots of conceptual development for students and faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student growth model and educational threads
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalize goals as educational threads integrated throughout courses. Initially five threads were: scientific computing, history of mathematics, communications, mathematical reasoning, and mathematical modeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threads provide consistent objectives across courses; courses write objectives to address each thread, enabling longitudinal assessment of growth across the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate content-specific threads for clearer assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulation of the student growth model into nine content threads: vectors, limits, approximation, visualization, models (discrete and continuous, linear and nonlinear, single- and multi-variable), functions, rates of change, accumulation, and representations of solutions (numerical, graphical, symbolic, descriptive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressing growth objectives in mathematical terms helps students and faculty identify expected growth and facilitates design of content-specific assessment instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common portfolio questions as required reflective tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Require responses to common questions each course (examples: 'Define a function...'; 'Discuss how a math modeling process is used...'), with each subsequent portfolio including earlier responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short typed paragraphs prompt synthesis and provide artifacts for assessing conceptual growth; examples given to standardize reflection across cohorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of technology, modeling, and group projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate technology and more group projects that require mathematical modeling, writing for synthesis, and peer-group interaction across courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration is a reform goal that can be assessed by project rubrics, portfolio evidence, and evaluation of student work that combines computational, modeling, and communication skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum content tradeoffs and coverage goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Design new curricula to cover targeted topics (e.g., linear algebra, discrete math, multivariable calculus) by integrating content and technology while accepting reduced emphasis on some traditional topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about losses and gains (which topics are de-emphasized). Use curricular mapping to ensure essential content threads remain and to justify tradeoffs to stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty involvement, consensus-building, and leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Informed and empowering leadership of department heads and consensus-building among senior faculty are key factors motivating successful implementation of curriculum change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan multi-year faculty engagement, write down articulated goals, and maintain leadership to institutionalize change and retain clarity despite faculty turnover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous evaluation and iterative improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Continue program evaluation (databases for cohorts, common attitude questions each semester, updating student growth models, changing texts and assessment instruments as needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ongoing data to inform mid-program and mid-course corrections; treat assessment as an iterative process tied to curricular decisions and faculty development.
